column1: What was the last film you saw and your conclusion was "This is the worst acting I have ever seen"? I recently stumbled into a film that, by its final curtain call, left me questioning the very art of performance. I walked into the cinema expecting a riveting narrative and characters bursting with life, yet what unfolded on screen was a parade of wooden, lifeless statues desperately trying to mimic human emotion. The actors delivered lines as if reciting a grocery list, devoid of any warmth or nuance. I couldn’t help but think, “This is the worst acting I have ever seen.” It reminded me of that uncanny moment when you realize the magic has long since fled from the screen, replaced by a mechanical repetition of clichés and overblown dramatics.  During the film’s slow march to oblivion, I found myself comparing its performances to those of talented thespians from the golden age of cinema, whose every gesture carried meaning. Here, though, every emotion was reduced to a series of exaggerated facial contortions and robotic pauses—a stark reminder that passion cannot be faked. It was as if the actors were reading from a script without ever understanding that acting, at its heart, is about believing in the words you're uttering.   I left the theatre feeling like I had just endured a crash course in method acting gone horribly astray. In a world where technology and CGI often steal spotlight, authentic human expression still ought to triumph. Yet, films like this seem to show an industry chasing trends rather than talent, rushing to cater to viewers’ short attention spans while sacrificing the rich tapestry of well-honed performances. Ultimately, that dreadful cinematic experience served as a poignant reminder: even in this era of innovation, there remains a timeless longing for genuine artistry on the silver screen.

What does a $1,500,000 house look like where you live? A $1,500,000 house where I live isn’t simply a showpiece of modern luxury, but rather an amalgamation of past and present, a bold statement of character mingled with the pragmatic realities of island life. Picture, if you will, a sprawling estate set amidst lush, tropical foliage—its design echoing both the sleekness of contemporary glass architecture and the enduring charm of colonial craftsmanship. The façade might boast expansive windows that invite in generous amounts of natural light, while subtle accents of timber lend the building a warmth that cold concrete structures often lack.  Step inside and you’re greeted by an interior that’s as much about function as it is about fashion. High ceilings and open spaces amplify the sense of airiness, while carefully curated art pieces hint at the owner’s appreciation for both local legends and international flair. Every room seems to tell its own story, balancing state-of-the-art technological conveniences with a nod to traditional craftsmanship—perhaps a carved wooden panel here, a vintage colonial lamp there.   Not to be overlooked is the outdoor space: an oasis of calm with meticulously designed gardens, a pool that shimmers like a sunlit lagoon, and perhaps even a secret nook for those moments when solitude calls. In a place where $1,500,000 might not always buy endless square footage, every inch of such a home is a calculated expression of pride and an ode to the unique blend of cultures that shape our surroundings.  It’s not merely about the monetary value, but the way this structure encapsulates the spirit of a community that values both progress and tradition—a rare balance that, when achieved, is nothing short of transcendent.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? I must confess that on more than one occasion I have engaged in what I now consider a small yet gratifying act of culinary retribution. I remember a time back in my early university years in Trinidad, when my flatmate developed an uncanny habit of pilfering my homemade treats right from the fridge. Instead of confronting him directly, I decided to turn the tables in a manner that was as harmless as it was ironically satisfying. I replaced the carefully prepared strawberry jam on my toast with a concoction laced with an extra dose of salt and an unexpected splash of vinegar. The face he wore as he took that first bite remains etched in my memory—a blend of confusion, regret, and a dash of comic disbelief.  It wasn’t a malicious act, mind you, but rather a subtle reminder that respect in shared spaces matters. Through that mischievous act, I reclaimed a shred of control over my personal domain. Culinary sabotage, as absurd as it might seem, brought a peculiar sense of balance to an otherwise chaotic living arrangement. In reflecting on that episode, I find myself amused by the whimsical ways in which we seek justice in everyday life, turning a simple meal into a declaration of self-respect. Perhaps, in the grand tapestry of existence, these small rebellions offer us a fleeting taste of liberty—a moment where ordinary ingredients are transformed into an unusual narrative of poetic justice. Who knew that a slice of toast could speak volumes about boundaries, trust, and the unexpected art of creative resistance? Similarly, every small act of defiance—however trivial—stands as an emblem of personal dignity and a quiet protest against tyranny. Every day.

What was your cringiest moment with a boss? I once experienced a cringeworthy moment with a boss that still leaves me shaking my head. It occurred on an ordinary Tuesday when our department was gathered for a routine meeting. Out of nowhere, my boss, known for his self-importance and bizarre attempts at authority, launched into a dramatic monologue about the “spirit of teamwork.” With theatrical gusto, he paced before us, his voice rising and falling as if reciting lines from a forgotten play. His performance was so overblown that colleagues exchanged looks of disbelief and discomfort. I distinctly remember a murmur spreading through the room, as if someone had punctured the bubble of decorum. In that moment, his attempt to seem inspirational instead felt like a desperate cry for validation.  He paused mid-sentence to adjust his tie—an action so exaggerated it seemed choreographed for a stage performance—and then resumed with even more flourish. Every intentionally placed gesture only deepened the absurdity of the situation. I felt mortified on behalf of my team, caught between forced admiration and incredulity. It was painfully clear that his grasp on authentic leadership was lost amidst theatrical grandstanding. My friends later joked that he was less a manager and more a misunderstood performer on a miscast stage. That day, the encounter served as a stark reminder that authority does not come from pomp and circumstance, but from genuine competency and humility.  Even now, when I recall that cringe-inducing display, it prompts me to reflect on how admirable qualities in a leader are far more than just superficial theatrics. I often share this episode with colleagues over coffee, a cautionary tale of misplaced grandeur and the perils of infusing business meetings with personal theatrics. It remains a defining moment in my professional memory indeed.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? I’ve often pondered this very question while sipping a bitter cup of local cocoa, wondering if life would be any less tangled without those miniature versions of ourselves running amok. On one hand, there’s an inexplicable joy in nurturing a seed that slowly unfurls into its own being—a living contradiction that forces you to confront your own imperfections daily. On the other hand, you might ask yourself, “Was the sacrifice of your solitude worth a lifetime of spilled juice and endless questions about why the refrigerator must always remain open?”   I remember once a friend—a self-proclaimed connoisseur of carefree living—asked if his freedom might be a form of regret. He claimed that while he relished the spontaneous adventures of star-gazing on a moonlit beach, a void lingered in the absence of a little one to call his own. But here’s the crux: regret is a two-edged blade. It seems that whether you choose the path of relentless responsibility or blissful liberation, each carries its own bittersweet aftertaste.   Perhaps it’s not a matter of presence or absence, but rather the willingness to embrace the often messy, unpredictable journey that defines us. Kids—or the lack thereof—are just one chapter in this sprawling narrative, a story punctuated by moments of heartache, laughter, and a touch of stubborn irony. In the end, the perpetual quest for meaning might just be less about what we gain or lose, and more about how we learn to dance amid life’s beautiful chaos.
